paragraph: At these words Dasaratha sorrowfully implored, "Do give up your anger against the Kshatriyas. Parasurama! "You are a brahmin of great austerities and renown. You, who should give refuge to my children, should not hurt them. Born in the venerable race of Bhargava, immersed in Vedic study, you had sworn to renounce your weapons in the presence of Indra. Dharmic that you are, you gave up the entire earth to Kasyapa, retiring to the solitude of the mountains. Does your arrival bode my destruction and that of my race? For none of us will live if Rama is killed".
Chapter/Canto/Verse_Reference: Bala Kanda, Sarga 75 (Dasaratha's Plea to Parasurama)
Situation/Problem_Faced: Dasaratha, witnessing Parasurama's formidable challenge to Rama, is overcome with fear and sorrow. He pleads with Parasurama, reminding him of his Brahminical duty to protect, his past vow to renounce weapons, and his righteous acts. Dasaratha expresses his dire fear for the survival of his race if Rama is harmed, highlighting the extreme vulnerability he feels as a father.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: This passage highlights Dasaratha's immense paternal love and desperate fear for Rama's safety. It portrays his attempt to appease Parasurama by appealing to his Brahminical virtues and past righteous conduct. Dasaratha's words demonstrate his understanding of Parasurama's nature and the potential consequences of his wrath. His plea underscores the sacred duty of a Brahmin to protect, not to destroy, and the perceived violation of this dharma by Parasurama's challenge.
Outcome/Resolution: Dasaratha, filled with sorrow and fear, implores Parasurama to abandon his anger against the Kshatriyas and not harm Rama. He reminds Parasurama of his Brahminical duties, his past vow to renounce weapons, and his righteous deeds, expressing his fear that his entire race would perish if Rama were killed.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Pitri-Dharma (Father's Duty - to protect his children)
Dharma (Righteousness - appeal to Parasurama's past adherence)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Dasaratha's desperate plea to Parasurama is an act of 'Pitri-Dharma' (father's duty) to protect his son. He appeals to Parasurama's 'Brahma Teja' (spiritual power) and past adherence to 'Dharma' (righteous conduct), urging him to transcend his 'Krodha' (anger) and fulfill his Brahminical role of providing refuge rather than inflicting harm. Dasaratha's fear of 'destruction of my race' signifies the grave spiritual stakes involved in this divine confrontation, as the fate of his righteous lineage rests on Parasurama's actions.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, Dasaratha is in a state of profound anxiety and fear, driven by overwhelming paternal love. His 'sorrowful imploring' and expressions of utter 'hopelessness' if Rama is harmed reveal the immense psychological burden of facing an invincible foe threatening his beloved son. He employs psychological appeals, reminding Parasurama of his virtuous past and his identity as a Brahmin, hoping to trigger empathy and activate Parasurama's 'emotional regulation' to curb his destructive 'anger'. This scene highlights the emotional vulnerability of even a powerful king when his deepest attachments are threatened.
